title: Intel’s Classiq Acquisition Connects Quantum Hardware with Software
author: M
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Intel has signed a definitive agreement to acquire quantum software developer Classiq, bringing together technologies that could make quantum computing easier to program and deploy. According to the announcement, the combination would unite Classiq’s automated algorithm synthesis platform with Intel’s silicon spin-qubit technology, cryogenic control electronics and existing quantum software.

The proposed acquisition gives Intel a path toward a full-stack quantum computing business, connecting application development with the hardware that executes quantum circuits. Closing is expected in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary conditions. Financial terms were not disclosed in the supplied release.

Classiq addresses a significant development challenge: translating high-level computational goals into efficient quantum circuits. Its platform automates that process, helping developers build applications without manually designing every circuit operation. It also supports hardware benchmarking, resource optimization and execution across different quantum platforms.

Why It Matters

Quantum computing needs more than improved qubits to become commercially useful. Developers also need tools that make complex hardware accessible, productive and adaptable. Classiq could provide an important bridge between Intel’s manufacturing capabilities and the researchers and enterprises developing quantum applications.

The announcement draws a useful parallel with electronic design automation. Just as EDA helped semiconductor engineers manage growing chip complexity, quantum design automation could help developers create increasingly sophisticated circuits while working within hardware constraints.

Combining software and hardware expertise also creates opportunities for closer optimization across the stack. Better coordination could help match algorithms to available resources and guide future hardware development.

Intel’s commitment to maintain Classiq’s hardware-agnostic integrations is particularly encouraging. It would preserve customer flexibility while supporting a broader quantum ecosystem.

The acquisition would not itself resolve quantum computing’s technical challenges. It would, however, strengthen Intel’s ability to turn progress in silicon-based quantum hardware into a more accessible platform for application development.
